title: 9. Streaming-first, event-driven architecture
summary: Business events published once to a durable log feed operational services and the analytical platform alike, with streaming jobs building medallion layers continuously.

blocks.text: 45.1 Context and the problem it solved

In a batch-first platform, analytics learns about the business hours later by extracting tables, while operational services integrate with each other through point-to-point APIs. Two integration systems describe the same facts (an order was placed, a payment failed) in different ways and at different speeds. Fraud checks, stock updates and customer notifications need those facts in seconds; dashboards end up a day behind.

A **streaming-first** architecture makes the **event log** the primary integration backbone. Every important state change is published once as an event to a durable, replayable log, usually Apache Kafka or a compatible service. Operational consumers (notification service, fraud engine) and analytical consumers (Flink jobs writing Iceberg, Snowpipe Streaming into Snowflake) read the same events. It generalises Kappa (chapter 40) from a processing pattern into an enterprise integration style.

blocks.caption: The log decouples producers from every consumer, operational and analytical.

blocks.text: Producers write events in one of two ways. With the **transactional outbox**, a service writes its business change and an event row to an outbox table in the same database transaction; a CDC connector (for example Debezium with its outbox event router) publishes that row to Kafka. This avoids the dual-write problem, where the database commit succeeds and the Kafka publish fails. With **plain CDC** (chapter 17), table changes are published as they are; easier to start, but consumers then depend on the internal table schema.

Kafka retains events for days or indefinitely (with tiered storage), so new consumers can start from the beginning and failed ones can replay. Flink jobs subscribe, process with event-time semantics and watermarks (chapter 20), and commit results to Iceberg on each checkpoint, typically every 1-5 minutes.

blocks.title: Flink SQL: Kafka topic with Avro schema into a bronze Iceberg table
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE order_events (
  order_id STRING,
  customer_id STRING,
  status STRING,
  amount DECIMAL(18, 2),
  event_time TIMESTAMP(3),
  WATERMARK FOR event_time AS event_time - INTERVAL '30' SECOND
) WITH (
  'connector' = 'kafka',
  'topic' = 'commerce.orders.v1',
  'properties.bootstrap.servers' = 'kafka:9092',
  'properties.group.id' = 'flink-orders-bronze',
  'scan.startup.mode' = 'group-offsets',
  'format' = 'avro-confluent',
  'avro-confluent.url' = 'http://schema-registry:8081'
);

CREATE CATALOG lake WITH (
  'type' = 'iceberg',
  'catalog-type' = 'rest',
  'uri' = 'https://catalog.internal/api/catalog'
);

INSERT INTO lake.bronze.order_events
SELECT order_id, customer_id, status, amount, event_time
FROM order_events;

The Iceberg sink commits when a Flink checkpoint completes, so the checkpoint interval is the freshness and small-file dial. One-minute checkpoints mean roughly 1,440 commits per day per table; schedule compaction accordingly (chapter 25).
45.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

The medallion model becomes a **streaming medallion**. Bronze is the raw event stream persisted to Iceberg, append-only. Silver is maintained continuously: Flink deduplicates by event id, applies late events within the watermark, and upserts current-state entities (an `orders` table from `order_*` events) into Iceberg using equality deletes or periodic MERGE. Gold may be streaming aggregates, but often remains micro-batch (chapter 19) because many business aggregates do not need second-level freshness.

items: **Events are facts.** Model topics as business events (`OrderPlaced`, `PaymentFailed`) with stable ids, an event time and a schema version. They map naturally to fact tables.
**Schema registry as contract.** Set compatibility (usually BACKWARD or FULL) per subject so producers cannot ship breaking changes; this is computational governance in practice.
**Keys and ordering.** Kafka orders only within a partition; key by entity id so all events for one order arrive in order.

**Snowflake:** Snowpipe Streaming lands rows in Snowflake tables within seconds; Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables as targets are also possible; check current documentation for supported targets and cost model.
**Semantic layer:** sits on gold Iceberg or Snowflake tables as usual; metric definitions must state their freshness so users know whether a number is seconds or hours old.

blocks.text: Ingestion is continuous, so orchestration changes character. Long-running Flink jobs are deployed and supervised (Flink Kubernetes Operator or a managed Flink service) rather than scheduled; Airflow or Dagster still runs compaction, snapshot expiry, batch gold models and backfills. Serving is split by latency: Snowflake and Trino for analytical queries over minutes-fresh tables, real-time OLAP (chapter 46) or a key-value store for sub-second, user-facing reads.

Replay is a feature only if consumers are idempotent. A Flink job restarted from an old offset will re-emit results; sinks must upsert on keys or rely on exactly-once commit protocols. Operational consumers such as an email service need their own deduplication, or customers receive the same message twice.

blocks.text: 45.7 When to choose it, and when not

items: Choose it when operational use cases (fraud, personalisation, logistics) already need events in seconds; analytics then reuses the same stream.
Choose it when engineering teams already run Kafka and can own event schemas as a product.
Choose it when many consumers need the same changes and point-to-point integrations are multiplying.
Avoid it when the only consumers are daily dashboards; batch or micro-batch is cheaper and simpler.
Avoid it when the team has no streaming operations experience and no managed services budget.
Mixed is normal: stream bronze and silver, keep heavy gold models in batch.

blocks.title: Food delivery platform
blocks.text: A delivery company published order, courier and payment events through outbox tables and Debezium into Kafka, with Avro schemas under BACKWARD compatibility. The dispatch service and fraud engine consume the topics directly. Flink writes bronze and silver Iceberg tables with two-minute checkpoints; finance's gold models run hourly in dbt; the operations dashboard reads from a real-time OLAP store fed by the same topics.
items: One definition of 'order delivered' for operations and finance
A schema change that removed a field was blocked by the registry before deploy
Replaying a week of events rebuilt a buggy silver table without touching sources

blocks.title: Move a batch platform to streaming-first
blocks.text: A subscription business loads its Postgres billing database nightly into Snowflake. Product wants churn-risk alerts within five minutes of a failed payment, and finance wants the existing reports unchanged. Design the event capture (outbox or CDC), topics and keys, schema compatibility policy, which layers stream and which stay batch, and how Snowflake receives the data. Describe how you would handle a consumer bug discovered after three days.
hints: Who owns the event schema if you use plain CDC?
Does finance gain anything from streaming gold?

items: Streaming-first makes a durable event log the shared backbone for operational and analytical consumers.
The transactional outbox avoids dual writes; plain CDC leaks internal schemas.
A schema registry with compatibility rules is the contract layer.
Streaming medallion: bronze and silver continuous in Iceberg, gold often micro-batch; Snowpipe Streaming feeds Snowflake.
Replay and exactly-once only help if sinks and consumers are idempotent.

blocks.q: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?
options: Kafka's lack of ordering across partitions
The dual-write problem where a database commit and a Kafka publish can diverge
blocks.explain: The event is written in the same transaction as the business change, then published by CDC, so both happen or neither. Ordering and small files are separate concerns.

blocks.q: A Flink job writes to Iceberg with 30-second checkpoints. What is the main side effect?
options: Many small files and snapshots, requiring frequent compaction and expiry
Events will be lost between checkpoints
blocks.explain: The Iceberg sink commits per checkpoint, so short intervals create many small commits. Events are not lost: uncommitted data is replayed from Kafka after failure.

blocks.q: Why key order events by order_id in Kafka?
options: To spread one order across all partitions for parallelism
So that all events for one order land in one partition and stay in order
blocks.explain: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition. Keying by entity id keeps each order's events ordered; spreading them would allow a cancellation to be processed before its creation.

blocks.q: Which situation least justifies a streaming-first architecture?
options: A company whose only data consumers are daily finance dashboards
Logistics tracking with live courier positions
Ten services integrating through point-to-point APIs on the same order data
Fraud detection needing payment events within seconds
blocks.explain: Streaming pays off when operational consumers need low latency or many systems share the same changes. Daily dashboards alone are served more cheaply by batch or micro-batch.
